question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t},4t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=4t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot 4 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{1}-4\cdot 1)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}-4) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t}⟩$ at the point $t=9.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y},-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=\sqrt{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(9))] & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{x}^{2},2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨3{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨3{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}-1 \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}-4}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},2t-1⟩$ at the point $t=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=2t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2{t}^{2},-2(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\cdot ⟨2t,2⟩ \\  & =2{t}^{2}\cdot 2t+(2-4t)\cdot 2 \\  & =4{t}^{3}-8t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =4(0)^{3}-8(0)+4 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t},3t-1⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t,y=\sqrt{t}$ and $z=3t-1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\sqrt{t}(3t-1),2t(3t-1),2t\sqrt{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩ \\  & =(3t-1)\sqrt{t}\cdot 2+(6{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+2t\sqrt{t}\cdot 3 \\  & =6t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}+6t\sqrt{t} \\  & =12t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =12(1)\sqrt{1}-2\sqrt{1}+\frac{3(1)^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,3t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=3t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨2,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{5}{1+25(1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25} \\  & =\frac{5}{26}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=\frac{1}{t},$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\cdot ⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩ \\  & =(-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 2t+(-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}

$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+z)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y},x{e}^{y},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=4,$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},4{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =t\cdot 0+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =4+{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =4+{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=3 x z^{2} - 3 y^{3}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨- 3 t,3,\sqrt{t^{2} - 3}⟩$ at the point $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3 x z^{2} - 3 y^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3 x z^{2} - 3 y^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂z}(3 x z^{2} - 3 y^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨3 z^{2},- 9 y^{2},6 x z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=- 3 t$, $y=3$, $z=\sqrt{t^{2} - 3}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨3 \left(\sqrt{t^{2} - 3}\right)^{2},- 9 \cdot 3^{2},6 \left(- 3 t\right) \sqrt{t^{2} - 3}⟩ \\  & =⟨3 t^{2} - 9,-81,- 18 t \sqrt{t^{2} - 3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 3 t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t^{2} - 3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 3}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨3 t^{2} - 9,-81,- 18 t \sqrt{t^{2} - 3}⟩\cdot ⟨-3,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 3}}⟩ \\  & =\left(3 t^{2} - 9\right)\cdot \left(-3\right)+\left(-81\right)\cdot \left(0\right)+\left(- 18 t \sqrt{t^{2} - 3}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 3}}\right) \\  & =- 9 t^{2} + 27+0- 18 t^{2} \\  & =- 27 t^{2} + 27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =- 27 (2)^{2} + 27 \\  & =-9+0-72 \\  & =-81.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=x^{2} - 2 y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨t,- 3 t + 1⟩$ at the point $t=1.$

The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

$$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute $x=t$, $y=- 3 t + 1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2 t,- 4 \left(- 3 t + 1\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨2 t,12 t - 4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 3 t + 1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2 t,12 t - 4⟩\cdot ⟨1,-3⟩ \\  & =\left(2 t\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(12 t - 4\right)\cdot \left(-3\right) \\  & =- 34 t + 12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =- 34 (1) + 12 \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨- t + 2,2 t⟩$ at the point $t=-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(- 3 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(- 3 x^{2} + 3 y^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨- 6 x,6 y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=- t + 2$, $y=2 t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨- 6 \left(- t + 2\right),6 \cdot 2 t⟩ \\  & =⟨6 t - 12,12 t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t + 2),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨6 t - 12,12 t⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2⟩ \\  & =\left(6 t - 12\right)\cdot \left(-1\right)+\left(12 t\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\  & =18 t + 12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & =18 (-1) + 12 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=3 x^{2} - 3 y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨- 3 t + 2,2 t - 1⟩$ at the point $t=-2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute $x=- 3 t + 2$, $y=2 t - 1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨6 \left(- 3 t + 2\right),- 6 \left(2 t - 1\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨- 18 t + 12,- 12 t + 6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 3 t + 2),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t - 1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨- 18 t + 12,- 12 t + 6⟩\cdot ⟨-3,2⟩ \\  & =\left(- 18 t + 12\right)\cdot \left(-3\right)+\left(- 12 t + 6\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\  & =30 t - 24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-2))] & =30 (-2) - 24 \\  & =-84.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=x^{2} - y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨- 3 t + 1,- t - 1⟩$ at the point $t=-2.$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute $x=- 3 t + 1$, $y=- t - 1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2 \left(- 3 t + 1\right),- 2 \left(- t - 1\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨- 6 t + 2,2 t + 2⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 3 t + 1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t - 1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-1⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} - 2 y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨t - 2,3 t + 2⟩$ at the point $t=0.$

The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute $x=t - 2$, $y=3 t + 2$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨- 6 \left(t - 2\right),- 4 \left(3 t + 2\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨- 6 t + 12,- 12 t - 8⟩\end{aligned}

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t - 2),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t + 2)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
